#### Learning Objectives

* Understand the aim and design of a typical subcellular proteomics experiment
* Understand De Duve's principle
* Understand the aim and design of the use-case DIA subcellular proteomics experiment
* Understand what DIA-NN does and what data it outputs for downstream analysis

:::

## Introduction to subcellular proteomics

The field of subcellular spatial proteomics is centered on the determination of
protein localisation within the cell. Importantly, protein localisation is
intimately linked to protein function and is vital for research into basic
biological mechanisms impacting the health and disease of all organisms.
Quantitative mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics methods have been developed
to study protein localisation at the proteome-wide level and generate
subcellular "maps". Several high throughput MS-based correlation profiling
methods have been established and include the Localisation of Organelle Proteins
(LOP) family of methods [@Sadowski2006; @Geladaki2019; @Christoforou2016;
@Kieran2025], dynamic organellar maps (DOMs) [@Itzhak2016], protein correlation
profiling (PCP) [@Foster2006], sequential detergent-based solubilisation
[@MartinezVal2021], COLA [@Mardakheh2017], Prolocate [@Jadot2017] and
SubcellBarCode [@Orre2019]. 

Generation of protein correlation profiling data requires considerable effort,
expense and well thought-out experimental designs for successful implementation.
Equally, data analysis involves considerable time and investment to produce high
quality, robust datasets which enables meaningful biological interpretation and
utility to the research community.

In this course material, we provide an updated workflow for the processing and
analysis of correlation profiling-based spatial proteomics data, based on our
f1000 workflow [@Hutchings2025]. We cover the key steps required to extract
spatial information from quantitative correlation profiling MS data. The first
step requires data importation, processing, and quality control followed by the
definition of subcellular markers. We discuss how to curate such markers using
approaches including unsupervised clustering and dimensionality reduction. Next,
we show how to use subcellular markers to generate spatial proteome maps. This
involves the classification of protein localisation through classical or
Bayesian semi-supervised machine learning algorithms using the [`pRoloc`
package](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/pRoloc.html).

## Software

In this workflow we use R packages from Bioconductor, namely, the
[`QFeatures` package](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/QFeatures.html)
for upstream data processing and the `pRoloc` for downstream 
machine learning. 

:::{.callout-note}
## MSnSets versus QFeatures data structures
In our first [F1000 workflow for spatial proteomics](https://f1000research.com/articles/5-2926) 
[@Breckels2018] we used the [`MSnbase` package](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/MSnbase.html) 
and the `MSnSet` infrastructure for storing and manipulating our spatial
proteomics data. In this workflow, we have transitioned to working with the 
`QFeatures` package for data processing. Whilst `MSnbase` provides functionality 
for manipulating and storing quantitative proteomics data, the `QFeatures` 
infrastructure makes it possible to store all levels of the data together in one 
object with explicit links maintained between hierarchical levels. For example,
it is possible to store the peptide spectrum matches (PSMs), peptides and proteins
(among other types of data) derived from all replicates of an experiment together,
in one single data container. 
:::

## The use-case: Subcellular mapping of U-2 OS cells using DIA-LOP

As a use-case, we will analyse a label-free DIA subcellular proteomics dataset
from a partially differentiated human osteosarcoma (OS) cell line (U-2 OS cells)
[@Kieran2025]. U-2 OS cells are one of the earliest described cancer derived cell lines and 
widely used across many areas of research. For subcellular proteomics they have
been widely used in benchmarking as they provide a robust, flat, epithelial-like
morphology and a deeply profiled human proteomic reference map.

Mass spectrometry (MS)-based protein correlation profiling data can be generated
using a number of methodologies. These methods can differ with respect to (1)
biochemical fractionation, (2) peptide quantitation (label-based or label-free),
and (3) mass spectrometry acquisition method (data-dependent acquisition, DDA,
or data-independent acquisition, DIA).

Our use-case data was generated using the DIA-LOP method from the Lilley lab at
the Universisty of Cambridge. DIA-LOP (Data-Independent Acquisition
Localization of Organelle Proteins), it is a next-generation subcellular
proteomics method that offers a faster, label-free, and cost-effective
alternative to classic multiplexed LOPIT methods. The pipeline works by gently
lysing cells and using differential ultracentrifugation to separate intact
organelles into 10 distinct fractions based on density. Instead of using
expensive chemical tags e.g. tandem mass tags (TMT), these fractions undergo
label-free peptide digestion and are analyzed via advanced DIA mass
spectrometry, which systematically fragments all ions to capture low-abundance
proteins from very low sample inputs. For each sample, a total of 750 ng of peptide
was analysed using using a timsTOF HT mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, 
Germany) coupled with a nanoElute 2 UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics). 

The data was processed using the freely available
[DIA-NN](https://github.com/vdemichev/DiaNN) software [@Demichev2019] for
peptide and protein identification and quantification, followed by the
Bioconductor
[QFeatures](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/QFeatures.html)
package to aggregate and process precursor-level data into robust protein
abundance profiles. Subsequently, the
[pRoloc](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/pRoloc.html)
package was used for protein subcellular localisation and the generation of
organelle maps, matching the abundance profiles of unknown proteins against
known organelle markers to map over 8,000 protein groups across subcellular
compartments. The raw MS data is available online through ProteomeXchange via
the PRIDE repository under the identifier [PXD063082](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/projects/PXD063082).

## Identification search of the raw MS data
Database searching of MS data involves comparing the observed MS spectra
to expected MS spectra generated via in silico digestion of a selected protein 
database. Since the use-case data used human cells, we provided the human proteome
to Proteome Discoverer as the database for searching. We also provided a 
database of common contaminants that could be present in our sample due to (i)
human contamination (e.g., keratin from nails, hair or skin), or (ii) sample
preparation (e.g., enzymes used for protein digestion). These two databases are
can be found in the course materials and also at
[](https://github.com/CambridgeCentreForProteomics/f1000_subcellular_dia_extension). The
result of such a database search is a list of **peptide spectrum matches (PSMs), or precursors**,  
that is a list of matches between observed and expected spectra. Most
software will also aggregate the PSM or precursor level data upward and provide output files
at all data levels (PSM, peptide and protein). It is up to the user which output
file to use for further analysis.

The starting point for this workshop and data processing workflow in R is an 
output file from the identification search. Different softwares output different
file formats, for example the Proteome Discoverer v3.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific)
outputs a `.txt` file format, as does [MaxQuant](https://www.maxquant.org), 
[FragPipe](https://fragpipe.nesvilab.org), other such as [DIA-NN](https://github.com/vdemichev/DiaNN) output
parquet formats, will will show in the subsequent section how to import such
data.
:::

## Which data level should you start from?

Proteomics search and quantification software can report results at several
levels: PSMs, precursors (a peptide sequence with its modifications and charge
state), modified peptides, peptide sequences, and protein groups. In general, we
recommend starting from the lowest level available. This gives you maximum
control over data quality filtering, normalisation and aggregation, and makes
each step of the analysis easier to understand and report transparently.

What "lowest level" means depends on the acquisition method. For TMT data
acquired by DDA, each MS2 spectrum is matched to a peptide, so analysis can
start from the PSM level. In DIA, MS2 spectra are chimeric and identification is
peptide-centric, so there are no PSMs and the lowest level is the precursor.
Some tools for label-free data also only accept peptide-level input, so starting
at the lowest level is not always possible.

The data we will use in this workshop is label-free DIA-LOP, so we will start
from the precursor level (rather than the PSM-level TMT data typical of DDA
LOPIT).

## Summary
The use-case data that we will process and analyse in this workshop is a **DIA**
**label-free** **LOP** subcellular proteomics dataset on human U-2 OS cells. The aim of the experiment is
to determine **where proteins reside in the cell** (their subcellular
localisation).

## Glossary

Key terms that you should understand for this workshop.

### Mass spectrometry basics

- **Precursor ion** = the intact, charged peptide ion that is selected for fragmentation. In analysis, a precursor is a unique combination of peptide sequence, modifications and charge state.

- **Fragment ion** = an ion produced by fragmentation of the precursor ion, thus only representing a fraction of the original peptide sequence (e.g. b and y ions).

- **MS1 spectrum** = a survey scan of all intact ions eluting at a given time, separated by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). Each peptide typically appears as an isotopic envelope of peaks, with intensities that can be used for quantification.

- **MS2 (MS/MS) spectrum** = a mass spectrum of fragment ions produced by fragmenting selected precursor ions, separated by m/z. In DDA, a spectrum usually comes from a single precursor; in DIA, it contains fragments from all precursors in an isolation window (a chimeric spectrum).

- **Isolation window** = the m/z range of precursor ions that is passed to the collision cell and fragmented together. In DIA, windows are typically several to tens of m/z wide and step across the full m/z range.

- **Chimeric spectrum** = an MS2 spectrum containing fragment ions from more than one precursor. DIA spectra are chimeric by design, which is why identification relies on specialised software rather than PSMs.

### Acquisition methods

- **Data-dependent acquisition (DDA)** = an acquisition mode in which the instrument selects the most abundant precursor ions from each MS1 scan and isolates and fragments them individually. Each MS2 spectrum therefore usually originates from a single precursor.

- **Data-independent acquisition (DIA)** = an acquisition mode in which all precursor ions within predefined m/z windows are fragmented together, without selecting individual precursors. This gives more complete and reproducible coverage across samples than DDA.

### Chromatography

- **Liquid chromatography (LC)** = the separation of peptides over time before they enter the mass spectrometer, which reduces the number of peptides being analysed at once.

- **Retention time** = the time at which a peptide elutes from the LC column. Peptides with the same sequence elute at reproducible times, which helps to identify them.

- **Extracted ion chromatogram (XIC)** = a plot of the intensity of a specific ion (precursor or fragment) against retention time. In DIA, precursors are identified partly because their fragment ion XICs peak together (co-elute).

### Identification and data levels

- **Peptide spectrum match (PSM)** = an assignment of an observed MS2 spectrum to a peptide sequence, based on how well it matches the theoretical spectrum of that sequence. PSMs arise from DDA data; DIA has no PSMs.

- **Spectral library** = a collection of reference spectra and retention times for peptides, used to search DIA data. Libraries can be built from DDA experiments or predicted in silico from sequence.

- **Peptide-centric search** = an identification strategy that asks whether the expected fragments of a given peptide are present in the data, as used in DIA. It contrasts with the spectrum-centric approach of DDA, where each spectrum is matched to a peptide.

- **Modified peptide** = a peptide sequence together with its post-translational or chemical modifications (e.g. oxidised methionine), regardless of charge state. One modified peptide can give rise to several precursors.

- **Protein group** = a set of proteins that cannot be distinguished from one another based on the identified peptides, which are reported together as a single entry.

- **False discovery rate (FDR)** = the expected proportion of incorrect identifications among those accepted. It is usually estimated with decoy sequences and controlled at a threshold such as 1%.

### Quantification and data processing

- **Label-free quantification (LFQ)** = quantification based on the measured signal of each peptide in each sample, without chemical labels. Each sample is acquired in a separate MS run.

- **Tandem mass tag (TMT)** = an isobaric peptide label used for relative quantification of peptides across samples. Labelled peptides from different samples have the same mass at MS1, and quantification is based on reporter ions released on fragmentation at the MS2 or MS3 level.

- **Isobaric labels** = tags with the same total mass that are indistinguishable at MS1 but release different reporter ions on fragmentation, which allows quantification across samples in the same run.

- **Reporter ion** = a low-mass fragment released from an isobaric tag whose intensity reports the relative abundance of a peptide in a given sample.

- **Missing value** = a peptide or protein that is not quantified in a sample. Missing values are common in proteomics, especially for low-abundance peptides, and are less frequent in DIA than in DDA.

- **Normalisation** = adjusting intensities to remove technical differences between samples or runs (e.g. loading amount), so that samples can be compared.

- **Aggregation (summarisation)** = combining lower-level measurements (e.g. precursors) into a higher level (e.g. proteins) using a method such as the median or a model-based approach.

### Spatial proteomics

- **Subcellular fractionation** = the partial separation of a lysate into fractions enriched in different organelles, usually by centrifugation.

- **Localisation of organelle proteins by isotope tagging (LOPIT)** = a spatial proteomics method that measures protein abundance across subcellular fractions, traditionally using TMT labels and DDA.

- **DIA-LOP** = the label-free DIA version of the same approach, in which fractions are acquired by DIA rather than labelled with TMT.

- **Abundance profile** = the pattern of a protein's abundance across fractions. Proteins in the same compartment tend to have similar profiles.

- **Marker protein** = a protein with a well-established subcellular location, used to define the expected profile of each compartment for classification.

- **Relocalisation** = a change in a protein's subcellular location between conditions (e.g. treated vs untreated), detected as a change in its abundance profile.
